title: Pico and Kettle's Whisperwind Win
markdown:
The Whisperwind Peaks wore their snow like hats they refused to take off. Rope ferries creaked between them, and on clear days the farmers’ sprite-bells made a thin orchestra in the mist. Down in Craggleton the air had the pitch of a hive someone had shaken. It was Peak-Plucking day: fetch the rarest flower from the upper ledges, or the strangest, or the one that made the judges forget they were old.

Grok the gnome had hired dwarves to drag a block of glacier through the street, intending to chisel out a frost-bloom that might not exist. Meltwater was already rehearsing rivers between the cobbles. Kitto Button, whose voice could have herded sheep from the next valley, had spent weeks staining his beard with berry juice until it looked “naturally weathered.” The juice had other ideas. The beard was going salmon in stripes.

Pico watched from the wobbly hut at the village edge and did not join the noise. He was a quiet goblin, which people mistook for a small one. His eyes were polished obsidian and they did not miss the way Grok’s ice was already surrendering or the way Kitto kept checking his reflection in shop windows. Pico’s fingers could tie a knot against a hurricane and undo it at a whisper. Beside him, Kettle the goat wore the golden-eyed expression of someone who had met humans and filed the experience under weather.

“Too much fuss,” Pico said. “The judges can smell effort. It is too obvious.”

Kettle removed a burr from his own beard and bleated the question.

“Win,” Pico said, “without anyone noticing I am trying.”

The Grand Caldera held the contest the way a bowl holds soup: elders on a platform, pine on the air, wind practising theft. The scent of the peaks was damp earth and cold resin, the sort of smell that makes a person stand up straighter without meaning to. The best blooms grew on ledges that could pluck a troll if the troll were foolish enough to pose. Pico wanted the Sky-Whisper Blossom, luminous, rumoured, said to keep to the sheerest face above the mist. Everyone in Craggleton knew the name. Almost no one liked the climb. Grok’s ice had become a sad lake, and the dwarves were arguing about invoices. Kitto was redyeing in a panic that suggested sunsets had gone wrong. A child asked if the beard was a prize. Kitto said it had wrestled a thundercloud. The child looked unconvinced.

Borris arrived the way a boulder arrives: slowly, and as if he had always been part of the slope. He was an ogre shepherd, not a villain, not a contestant. His beard was moss that had learned patience. Most days he watched a lost tuft of wool as if it contained a philosophy. Today the wool lost. His gaze drifted, without hurry, to Pico and Kettle, who were loafing with the particular stillness of people who have already done the work.

For weeks Pico had been building a thing that looked like a bird’s nest if the bird had studied sails. Angled cloth. A weighted hook. He said, just loud enough for a gossip to inherit, that the Sky-Whisper had to be on the Whispering Ledge. Kettle nodded once, the nod of a goat who has already agreed with the physics.

Borris’s eyes, usually half-shut, opened all the way.

Pico carried the nest to a windy lip above the caldera and let go. The thing did not swoop. It drifted as if it had forgotten a better plan. Kettle nudged a sail. Pico’s fingers made a correction too small to photograph. The hook found the luminous cluster the way a thought finds the right word. Pico tugged. Kettle shoved. The blossoms came down in a rustle that landed at Pico’s boots. From the stands it was weather. Lucky weather. The pretty kind.

Elder Maeve sat up as if someone had passed her a secret. Pico shrugged the shrug of a person who has been tripped over by fortune.

“Remarkable,” she said. “Retrieved with such ease.”

Then the ground made the sound of stones conferring. Borris stepped forward, and Craggleton, which was used to his silence, discovered it had been waiting for this sentence.

“He did not just get them.” The finger, when it pointed, found Kettle first. “The goat. Nudging the sails. Guiding it.” Then Pico. “The goblin faked the wind. Planned it.”

Murmur, the cheap kind. Pico’s face did a rare unguarded thing. He had counted on ice and beards and had not budgeted for a shepherd who actually looked.

Borris’s expression gentled, which on an ogre is a weather change. “Winning is not always the loudest work. Sometimes it is knowing what you can do, and who helps you do it. They did not perform the mountain. They used it.”

The judges glanced at one another and found, to their own surprise, that they were not in the mood for a riot. Maeve’s voice came down a notch.

“Elegantly executed,” she said. “The terrain, the resources, and a quite remarkable companion. The Sky-Whisper Blossom. Exquisite.”

Pico won the way a door closes: without a brass band. Villagers left still tasting Borris’s voice. Pico scratched the warm place behind Kettle’s ear. The goat blinked, unimpressed on principle, and bleated as if to say the nest had been obvious from the start.

Above them the Whispering Ledge kept its remaining flowers. Grok’s puddle reflected a scrap of sky. Kitto’s beard, in the late light, had settled on a colour no berry had intended. Pico did not make a speech. He picked a single fallen petal off Kettle’s shoulder, turned it once, and put it in his pocket as if that were the whole prize.
characters: Pico (quiet goblin with obsidian eyes), Kettle (a goat with unimpressed golden eyes)
audience: teenagers aged 13-15, amusing distant-lands fantasy for independent readers
